title: How Do Solar Panels Work? A Simple Guide for Homeowners
seoTitle: How Do Solar Panels Work - Homeowner Guide 2026
excerpt: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic cells. Learn how they work, what they cost, and what the 30 percent federal tax credit covers in 2026.
content:
How Do Solar Panels Work?

Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic (PV) cells made primarily from silicon. When sunlight hits a PV cell, it knocks electrons loose from silicon atoms, creating an electric current. This direct current (DC) electricity flows to an inverter, which converts it to alternating current (AC) for use in your home.

What Are the Main Parts of a Solar Panel System?

A residential solar system includes several key components. Solar panels capture sunlight and generate DC electricity. An inverter converts DC to AC electricity. A mounting system secures panels to your roof or ground rack. Wiring and conduit connect everything safely. A net meter tracks electricity sent to and drawn from the grid.

How Much Electricity Can Solar Panels Generate?

Most residential solar panels produce between 350 and 450 watts each under ideal conditions. A typical 6-kilowatt home system generates about 7,000 to 9,000 kilowatt-hours per year, enough to cover most or all of an average household's electricity use. Actual output depends on roof orientation, shading, local weather, and seasonal daylight hours.

What Is the Federal Tax Credit for Solar in 2026?

The Residential Clean Energy Credit covers 30 percent of the cost of a solar panel system, including equipment and installation, with no upper limit. The credit applies to systems installed through 2032 under current law. You claim it on your federal tax return using IRS Form 5695. Some states and utilities offer additional rebates or performance-based incentives.

How Long Do Solar Panels Last?

Most solar panels come with 25-year performance warranties and continue producing electricity well beyond that timeframe. Panel output typically declines by about 0.5 percent per year, meaning panels still operate at roughly 85 to 90 percent of original capacity after 25 years. Inverters usually need replacement after 10 to 15 years.

What Is Net Metering and How Does It Work?

Net metering credits you for excess electricity your panels send to the grid. When your system produces more than you use, the meter runs backward and you receive a credit on your bill. At night or on cloudy days, you draw electricity from the grid and use those credits. Policies vary by state and utility, so check your local rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does a residential solar system cost?

The average cost of a residential solar panel system in the United States is about $2.50 to $3.50 per watt before incentives. For a 6-kilowatt system, that is roughly $15,000 to $21,000 before the 30 percent federal tax credit, which brings the net cost down to approximately $10,500 to $14,700.

Do solar panels work on cloudy days?

Yes. Solar panels produce electricity on cloudy days, though at reduced output typically 10 to 25 percent of normal production depending on cloud cover. Panels still generate power from diffuse sunlight, not just direct sun.

Can I install solar panels myself?

DIY installation is possible but not recommended for most homeowners. Permitting, electrical work, roof mounting, and utility interconnection require specialized knowledge. Most jurisdictions require a licensed electrician to sign off, and manufacturer warranties may be voided by self-installation.

How long does it take to break even on solar panels?

The typical payback period for a residential solar system is 7 to 12 years, depending on system cost, local electricity rates, incentives, and sunlight. After the payback period, the electricity your panels produce is essentially free for the remainder of their 25-plus-year lifespan.

Do solar panels increase home value?

Research from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that homes with owned solar systems sell for a premium of about $15,000 on average compared to comparable homes without solar. Leased systems typically do not add the same value because buyers must assume the lease.

What happens to solar panels at the end of their life?

Solar panels are recyclable, though recycling infrastructure is still developing in the United States. Most panels contain glass, aluminum, copper, silicon, and small amounts of silver and lead. Several manufacturers and specialty recyclers offer take-back programs, and the Department of Energy supports solar recycling research.

Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (as of November 2026); National Renewable Energy Laboratory (as of November 2026); Solar Energy Industries Association (as of November 2026); Internal Revenue Service, Form 5695 instructions (as of November 2026).
